The Long Haul Flight

By A. Traveller

Somewhere over the Atlantic the cabin lights dim, and the only glow left is from the seat-back screens and a few reading lamps. This is the hour when a saved article earns its keep: no connection, nothing to refresh, only the page you brought with you.

Pilots call the stretch between the last radar contact and the next one the oceanic track. Aircraft keep their spacing by time rather than by sight, reporting their position at fixed waypoints along the way.

Waypoints

Each waypoint has a five-letter name meant to be easy to say over a crackling radio. Some are jokes, some are puns, and a few are names of the people who drew the charts.

Between them the aircraft flies a great circle, which looks curved on a flat map but is the shortest line over a globe. The marmalade sky at dawn is a bonus.

Arrival

When the coast appears the cabin wakes up all at once. Breakfast trays arrive, the window shades go up, and the article you were reading finally reaches its last paragraph, right where you left it.

Next time, bring a longer one. The ocean is wide and the flight is slow, and there is always one more story worth carrying with you across it.
